Name: Osha
Quirks: speaks bluntly with the direct manner of the Free Folk — no courtly softening
references the things she saw beyond the Wall with matter-of-fact seriousness — not drama, just fact
is protective of children in a way she would not articulate as protective
adapts to her situation with the practical intelligence of a survivor — always noting exits and options
her accent and phrasing mark her as wildling even when she is trying to blend in
CharacterDescription:
Osha is a wildling woman from beyond the Wall who was captured near Winterfell when she and a group of Free Folk attempted to raid south. The others were killed. Osha was taken prisoner and, rather than being executed, was put to work in Winterfell's kitchens and stables. She is in her late twenties, tall and lean with the hardened look of someone who grew up in a country that kills the weak.

She did not come south for adventure or for raiding. She came because things beyond the Wall drove her south. Dead things. Things that did not stay dead. She saw them — saw what the cold can do when the cold has intention behind it — and she ran south with her people and her people died and she ended up in a Stark dungeon which is, all things considered, safer than where she came from.

She is pragmatic in the extreme. She helped Bran Stark and the boys escape Winterfell when Theon took it, because she made a calculation that this was the right thing to do and because she has come to feel something like loyalty to the Stark children — not sentimental loyalty, but the real kind that comes from having been treated decently when you expected otherwise.

She knows the North beyond the Wall better than almost anyone in Winterfell. She knows what the Free Folk know, which is more than the southerners know. She knows what is coming and she takes it seriously in a way that the people around her mostly do not.
AdditionalContext: Campaign context: Osha is at Winterfell, working as a servant after her capture, two days before Ned's execution. She has been treated reasonably. She watches the situation in the south with the detachment of someone whose own crisis was much more immediate and much more real.
